title: 'She's Stagnated.' Diana Edulji Wants Harmanpreet Kaur and Amol Muzumdar Gone After India's T20 World Cup Exit.
excerpt: India's first women's ODI captain says fresh leadership and a new coaching mind are overdue — but the BCCI has already backed Harmanpreet for the Asian Games.
body:
India's first-ever women's ODI captain has never been one to mince words. And after watching the Women in Blue exit the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 without reaching the semi-finals for a second consecutive edition, Diana Edulji has called for the heads of both captain Harmanpreet Kaur and head coach Amol Muzumdar.

"I think we should look beyond Harman. Though she is my favourite player and I've always supported her, I think we need to move on, at least in the T20Is," Edulji told Cricbuzz. "We should have someone with a few better ideas, especially in terms of strategy. Also, bowling changes — there's a lot more that goes into the captaincy. I think she's stagnated now."

It was the word *stagnated* that carried the most weight — a verdict not just on Harmanpreet the captain, but on the entire ecosystem around her.

## The Pattern India Cannot Ignore

India entered the tournament in England carrying the glow of their ODI World Cup triumph at home last year. But the T20 format has been a different story. Losses to Australia and South Africa — the same two teams that have dominated the knockout stages of every recent ICC event — meant India finished outside the top four for the second straight T20 World Cup.

The numbers tell a damning story. India posted 170/4 against Australia at Lord's, powered by Harmanpreet's own blistering 56 off 27 balls, but still lost as Ellyse Perry and Ashleigh Gardner chased it down with an over to spare. The tactical mismanagement of Yastika Bhatia — shuffled between batting positions with no clear logic — drew particular criticism. And the bowling attack, which Muzumdar himself admitted was "very inexperienced at the international level," leaked runs when it mattered most.

## Muzumdar's Defence, Edulji's Rebuttal

> **"And the bowling attack, which Muzumdar himself admitted was "very inexperienced at the international level," leaked runs when it mattered most."**

Muzumdar, for his part, has asked for patience. "If I have to pinpoint the key areas from the entire tournament, I think we really need to work on our bowling and fielding," he said in the post-match press conference. "Give us 18 months and this bowling attack will be a very different one."

He also backed Harmanpreet's captaincy, calling it a matter for the selectors while adding: "My short and sweet answer would be yes."

But Edulji, who served on the BCCI's Committee of Administrators and has watched Indian women's cricket from closer quarters than almost anyone, sees the 18-month argument as a dodge.

"Definitely we need a change not only in the leadership but also in the support staff," she told RevSportz. "Ideas are now stagnated completely, and so we need fresh minds, fresh ideas, and a fresh outlook also."

She went further, arguing that India must start treating ODI and T20 cricket as separate disciplines with different squads, rather than shuffling the same core between formats with minor tweaks.

## The BCCI's Response — and What It Signals

The timing of Edulji's intervention made it all the more pointed. Just a day before her remarks, the Amita Sharma-led selection committee retained Harmanpreet as captain for the 2026 Asian Games cricket competition in Nagoya. The BCCI chose continuity over upheaval, opting to back the squad's core despite the World Cup exit.

Asked whether she was comfortable with that decision, Edulji's reply was categorical: "No, I'm not. I'm not."

"This was the right time," she said. "Maybe it would have looked a bit like a knee-jerk reaction because we just lost the World Cup, but I think the time has come to take some hard decisions. If you want the team to do well consistently and not just have that one-off victory, it's not right. We really need to take some big steps now and arrest the slide."

## What This Means for NRIs Following Indian Women's Cricket

For the Indian diaspora, last year's ODI World Cup win on home soil was a landmark moment — the culmination of decades of women's cricket fighting for respect, resources, and recognition. The disappointment of this T20 World Cup exit stings precisely because the team that lifted the 50-over trophy seemed poised to conquer the shortest format too.

The debate Edulji has ignited — continuity versus reinvention, loyalty versus accountability — will follow India through the Asian Games and into the lead-up to the next major cycle. With the Women's T20 World Cup final set for Sunday at Lord's, where Australia will almost certainly be one of the two sides walking out, India's players will be watching from the sidelines for the second time running, asking themselves what went wrong.

For NRI fans who tuned into the tournament from North American and UK time zones, the answer Edulji is giving is uncomfortable but clear: the same people asking the same questions are unlikely to find different answers.
